messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Randomness during adapting causing slow sampling for chains in parallel?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Randomness during adapting causing slow sampling for chains in parallel?
messages.body_plain:
> Ah OK, I have tried using the same initial values for all chains, which does seem to help, but I think I might be getting bit by this randomness. Are there any plans to be able to control these, or at least seed these in some way so they start the same in all chains?

If the random numbers in each chain are the same (as would be the case given identical seeds) then the dynamics would be the same and you'd just get n copies of a single chain.

The big problem here is that if you start adaptation away from the typical set and your tails are heavy then there's always a chance of the adaptation going askew.  Starting all chains at the same point helps only if that point is close to the typical set (models that seem to be "well written" are often defined such that the origin is within the typical set, which is why --init=0 performs so well most of the time).  The easiest fix right now should be running Stan without any warmup, record the final value (you should see some convergence in the trace plots), and then use that to seed a full adaptation/sampling run.

We're currently working on more robust adaptation mechanisms.

On 7/1/13 9:15 AM, Ryan wrote:

>     Then NUTS is run during adaptation, and that has several kinds
>     of built-in randomness, including initial momentum and the directions
>     in which to update and a final Metropolis reject step.
>

> Ah OK, I have tried using the same initial values for all chains, which does seem to help, but I think I might be
> getting bit by this randomness. Are there any plans to be able to control these, or at least seed these in some way so
> they start the same in all chains?

The improvements we have planned are:

   * introducing an init block in the Stan language itself

   * allowing partial initializations, with other parameters being random

   * introducing additional randomness around inits

   * controlling how much extra randomness is added to the inits

All of this can be done in R before calling Stan, but the partial inits
are particularly problematic because we currently require either all or nothing
inits that are in the support of the posterior on the constrained scale.

As Michael mentioned, we've been thinking about more robust initialization
strategies (robust in the sense of getting to the first effective sample
more quickly and finding adaptation parameters that mix well from there).

These are high enough priority that they should actually happen :-)

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 6/30/13 9:54 AM, Allen Riddell wrote:
> Hi stan-users,
>
> After getting the horseshoe prior working without any problems, I found myself
> wondering about BMA. Is there a model resembling BMA that works in Stan? (I'm
> thinking about linear regression with p>50.)

We don't support BMA as such.

Instead, you can implement a mixture over models directly within Stan
and estimate the mixing rate at the same time.  This won't do hard
variable selection for you, though.

There's a chapter on mixtures in the manual with examples.  It's
a bit complicated because you have to marginalize out the discrete
parameters in an arithmetically stable way.  The marginalization also
helps sampling efficiency by computing with an expectation instead of
a sample.

By horseshoe, do you mean this?

   ftp://ftp.stat.duke.edu/pub/WorkingPapers/08-31.pdf

If so, did you use one of the latent parameter formulations
(lambda or kappa) or find a way to express the probability function
more directly?

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 7/2/13 5:12 PM, Kevin wrote:
> These questions are straight from the FAQ, so apologies in advance if there's an obvious answer. I'm trying to implement
> some of the suggestions in the "How can I speed up my code?" section of the FAQ, but running into issues.
>
> Consider the following toy rstan example:
>
> ################################
> n = 10
> d = 3
> m = 2
>
> t1 = matrix(rnorm(n*m),n,m)
> t2 = matrix(rnorm(m*d),m,d)
> x = t1%*%t2
> datalist = list(n=n,d=d,x=x,m=m)
>
> code <- '
>    data {
>      int<lower=1> n;
>      int<lower=1> d;
>      int<lower=1> m;
>      real x[n,d];
>    }
>    parameters {
>      real alpha[n,m];
>      real beta[m,d];
>    }
>    model {
>      real S[n,d];
>      alpha ~ normal(0,1);
>      beta ~ normal(0,1);
>
>      S <- alpha * beta;
>
>      for (i in 1:n)
>        for (j in 1:d)
>          x[i,j] ~ normal(S[i,j],1)
>    }
> '
>
>
> fit <- stan(model_code = code, data = datalist,
>         iter = 400, warmup = 100, chains = 1)
> ################################
>
> There are two issues here. First, I cannot apply the normal prior to the parameter matrices alpha and beta. I get this:
> DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
> no matches for function name="normal_log"
>      arg 0 type=real[2]
>      arg 1 type=int
>      arg 2 type=int
> available function signatures for normal_log:
> 0.  normal_log(real, real, real) : real
> [truncated]
>
> However, it works just fine if I replace it with the (presumably) slower version:
> ######
>      for (i in 1:n)
>        for (j in 1:d)
>          alpha[i,j] ~ normal(0,1);
> ######

We've only vectorized one level deep.  So you can have
1D arrays, but not matrices.  So what would work is this:

  for (n in 1:n)
    alpha[n] ~ normal(0,1);

> Second, the matrix multiplication does not seem to want to work. The "S <- alpha * beta;" line gives me this:
> DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
> no matches for function name="multiply"
>      arg 0 type=real[2]
>      arg 1 type=real[2]
> available function signatures for multiply:
> 0.  multiply(real, real) : real
> [truncated]
>
> Again, replacing it with the slower scalar operation version works just fine.
>
> Any idea what my problems are? Thanks

Here you're trying to plug a 2D array into a matrix operation.
Declare them as:

   parameters {
     matrix[n,m] alpha;
     matrix[m,d] beta;
   }

and the multiplication should do what you expect.  And similarly
declare S as an (n x d) matrix.

- Bob

No :-)  With p = 50, if you want models to be identified
by subsets of predictors, there's no way to marginalize explicitly.

Without discrete parameters, there's not a good
way to have a prior that has a finite probability mass
at 0 --- I'd think it would be challenging even with discrete
parameters.

It looks like you're already looking at various forms of
shrinkage, which should work just as well predictively.

With matrix objects, it's a bit more efficient to pull
out by column (even though the indexing notation only
supports rows).  That's because the underlying matrix lib
we use, Eigen, organizes matrices by column (by default,
which is what we went with).  Arrays of row vectors
(or arrays of vectors) are more efficient because there's
no copying needed.

> Just to clarify, "e0bds" is a matrix[Ndom, Ntot]. Will "e0bds ~ normal(0,1)" sample for the whole matrix if I replace it

No.  Sorry.  I didn't realize that one was a matrix.

We'll get there eventually, but it doesn't work yet.
But it's not that much overhead to call once per row,
especially if the rows are long.

On 7/9/13 11:46 AM, kris2...@gmail.com wrote:
> Is there a Probit function in stan? I need to get quantiles from a normal distribution, but all I seem to find are the
> normal cdf and erf rather than their inverses. Thanks

Section 11.4 of the manual explains how to do logit and
probit GLMs.  And 11.3 is on robit :-)

You have both Phi and the normal CDF.  Phi will be a bit
more efficient and more idiomatic, so it's what we used
in the manual examples.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Graded Response Model
messages.body_plain:
We put that message in for diagnostic reasons and it's been confusing
users ever since.

What is happening is that the leapfrog integrator used for simulating the
Hamiltonian dynamics (path of parameters over time under random initial momentum and
negative log probability potential energy) is based on a discrete time interval
and low-order approximation to the true curvature of the log prob function;  when the time
interval (i.e., step size) is too large, a step in the direction of the
momentum can take you out of the support for a function.

The message usually arises because of overflow or underflow, which can
help diagnosing a poorly specified model (not an error per se, but perhaps
a poor choice of priors or variable constraints).

In your case, the first message may indicate that the parameter in question
doesn't have the appropriate constraints defined, but not necessarily.  With
an ordered variable, a big enough random momentum step can destroy the
ordering.

What should happen is that adaptation should find a smaller time interval (step
size) and the messages should go away, or at least become relatively infrequent.
It can actually be optimal for them to keep showing up because we want to
balance larger time intervals for computational efficiency with Metropolis
rejection for sampling efficiency.

- Bob

messages.subject: Error message
messages.body_plain:
Bob,

The error message is fairly clear to me, and I think the information needs to be preserved for the user, even if not printed immediately.

If you can eliminate the first part (the warning that an error is coming) and the second part (the error) entirely, I'd say it would be good to have three counters in STAN: one in which iteration the error first occurs, one in which iteration the error last occurs, and one that counts how many times the error occurred. Then, at the end of a run, print a warning that lists these three counters. and refers the user to some pithy advice in the manual. (Maybe something like, "If the error occurs once and it is on the first iteration, you're probably okay, but should check the constraints of your parameters, looking for boundary conditions like lower=0 when the parameter should be strictly greater than zero. If the error occurs more than once, this is a sign of instability in ...")

Speaking of which, I notice that in various examples in the manual, you use <lower=0> when it appears that the value should be strictly greater than zero. I usually put <lower=0.001> in such situations. Is this correct, or am I confused?

messages.body_plain:
On 7/10/13 5:55 PM, Wayne Folta wrote:
> Bob,
>
> The error message is fairly clear to me, and I think the information needs to be preserved for the user, even if not
> printed immediately.
>
> If you can eliminate the first part (the warning that an error is coming) and the second part (the error) entirely, I'd
> say it would be good to have three counters in STAN: one in which iteration the error first occurs, one in which
> iteration the error last occurs, and one that counts how many times the error occurred. Then, at the end of a run, print
> a warning that lists these three counters. and refers the user to some pithy advice in the manual.

This would be very hard to build into the interface
without really cluttering things up for handling this
particular message.  I'd rather just print it every
iteration as we do.

The embedded "error" is the message thrown by the
distribution code that's called.  That really shouldn't
change, either.  We want to print it.  It should probably
say "exception", but that seems awfully programming-language
oriented to report back to a user.

> (Maybe something
> like, "If the error occurs once and it is on the first iteration, you're probably okay, but should check the constraints
> of your parameters, looking for boundary conditions like lower=0 when the parameter should be strictly greater than
> zero. If the error occurs more than once, this is a sign of instability in ...")

Sounds good.

> Speaking of which, I notice that in various examples in the manual, you use <lower=0> when it appears that the value
> should be strictly greater than zero. I usually put <lower=0.001> in such situations. Is this correct, or am I confused?

If you have

   real<lower=0> sigma;

then the lower=0 is theoretically an exclusive lower bound and the
constrained variable should be in the open interval (0,+infinity).

In this case, if the unconstrained parameter is sigma_raw, then
sigma = exp(sigma_raw).  Now exp() always returns a positive value
in theory.  Unlike for real numbers, in double-precision floating
point, if sigma_raw < -800 or so, exp(sigma_raw) will underflow and return 0.
It'll overflow to +infinity if sigma_raw > 800 or so.  (+infinity is
a valid floating point value in C++ and hence in Stan.

We've also extended some of the distributions to deal with
boundaries of 0 or +infinity or -infinity.  That part of the
code could stand to be cleaned up in terms of tests and
making sure all the boundary behaviors are as general as possible.

- Bob

messages.subject: out-of-sample predictions

I've been writing R functions to take the sample of coefficients and recapitulate the Stan model with arbitrary data, but it has become onerous to keep the stan code and R code in sync.

My model is essentially a logistic regression with nonlinear terms -- want predictions for a binomial response var.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] out-of-sample predictions
messages.body_plain:
Use the generated quantities block.  You can have random
functions of parameters and data and it's only computed
once per saved sample.

There's as of yet no good way to prevent the duplication
of the likelihood part of the model to generate new data.

For cross-validation, though, you need to have something
higher level to divide up the data into folds, but
each model itself can do predictive inference using
the generated quantities block.

For a logistic regression hard coded with a quadratic of
a single predictor, you'd do this:

data {
   ... as before ...
   int<lower=0> N_twiddle;       // # of points to predict
   vector[N_twiddle] x_twiddle;  // data for which to make predictions
}
parameters {
   ... as before ...
}
model {
   ... as before ...
}
generated quantities {
   vector[N_twiddle] y_hat_twiddle;  // predictions
   for (n in 1:N_twiddle)
     y_hat_twiddle[n] <- inv_logit(beta0 + beta1 * x_twiddle[n] + beta2 * beta2 * x_twiddle);
}

This saves the probabilities in y_hat_twiddle, but you might want
to do sampling, depending on the application, in which case you could
do:

    y_hat_twiddle[n] <- bernoulli_rng(inv_logit(...as above...));

where bernoulli_rng generates a binary value which is 1 with the
specified probability.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for sharing.  We have an effort going there to
implement all of the Gelman and Hill models that those actually
doing it can fill you in on (Alexeij?  Daniel?).

We plan to use our optimizers to recreate the functionality of
lmer (bglmer) max marginal estimates in Stan.  And of course
to get all the BUGS models working.

I'd highly recommend separating three things by file:

    1.  Stan model

    2.  data set

    3.  R code for fitting model & plotting results

By having 1 and 2 in separate files, Stan users who don't use R
will benefit.  And it makes it easier to browse the model
implementations.

As is, you have multiple models in a single R file.

Your code should run out of the box, either by including
copies of the data or using URLs.  As is, you have the
URL code commented out and a dangling local reference.

In general, you shouldn't have commented out alternative code
included with the actual code --- it's just confusing for users.
If there are two ways to do thing, put them both in the code
and have some way to configure them.  If not, remove the one
that's not needed.

There's also the choice of whether to do data transformations in
Stan or in the calling program (R in this case).  Either the transform
should be done to create the data set that's included or it should
be done in Stan in order to preserve the standalone nature of
model+data.

- Bob

It might also be some sort of interaction with the R.cache package (which I had never used before). There are a bunch of error messages that come up before the segfault that also do not appear to have anything to do with RStan but might suggest the root of problem.

Anyway, you can poke around under GDB some more, maybe Google some of these error messages, ask on the Rcpp list, etc. If you can simplify it down a lot more and / or produce something that more convincingly points to a problem in RStan, then we can look at it more closely.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Segfault with R.cached model
messages.body_plain:
As Ben pointed out, you can first try not to use R.cache package, which is not necessary at all when using RStan.  Sampling can always be done for a compiled model with different data and other inputs so compiling is needed just once for the same model.

And I am afraid that the problem is that R.cache does not handle objects created in RStan, which has a dynamic shared object created from compiling the C++ code.  From the description, I guess that after the dynamic shared object was unloaded by R (this happens automatically by R at a time that is not determined by the user), R.cache cannot load the dynamic shared object and thus a segfault follows.

--
Jiqiang

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Segfault with R.cached model
messages.body_plain:
My guess is not quite right about why the segfault happens.  But the problem does has to do with package R.cache and R's garbage collector.

The problem with using R.cache is that every time it loads the cache, the same DSO (though with different file names) would be loaded again, which seems to cause some problem (I still do not know why it is problematic and that is why now in RStan if you compile the same model from its Stan code the generated DSO will be different).  The following R code would always create this type of segfault.  So my advice for this problem is not to use package R.cache.

library(rstan)
library(R.cache)
testcode <- '
 parameters {
   real y;
 }
 model {
   y ~ normal(0, 1);
 }
'

sm <- stan_model(model_code = testcode)
k <- list(code = testcode)
saveCache(sm, key = k)
rm(sm)
base::gc()

sm <- loadCache(key = k)
f <- sampling(sm, chains = 1, iter = 10)

sm2 <- loadCache(key = k)
f2 <- sampling(sm2)
rm(sm2)
rm(f2)
gc()
rm(f)
gc()

--
Jiqiang

messages.subject: Re: Segfault with R.cached model
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for your thoughtful replies, folks.

My use for R.cache is to avoid having to recompile a model each time I start up R. I *can* simply avoid reloading the cached copy of the model once the current R process has done it once, and I found that if I do this, I can avoid segfaults in my original analysis (hooray!). But, if I understand correct, this still isn't entirely safe. I assume that using the stock save() and load() would be no better. Is there then no officially supported way to avoid recompiling the model for each R process? I opine that there should be. Compilation isn't fast.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Compiling Rstan under clang++ (c++11)
messages.body_plain:
Bob,

A couple of weeks ago we exchanged some emails about this subject and you suggested to see if this is a 'stan' problem or possibly in the Boost Spirit Qi (BSQ) parser. Some testing confirmed it is a parsing issue. Under O_STANC = 3 even the very first "data {..." was not recognized.

To make this problem reproducible, I ended up simplifying it all the way down to 2 grammars, a program-grammar and a whitespace-grammar which still show the problem. The resulting 'simplfied' source tree can be found at https://github.com/goedman/clang11-spirit-qi .

The whitespace-grammar is identical to the one used in Stan. The simplified program-grammar has very little to do anymore with Stan's syntax (but you'll recognize it :-).

It parses fine under O = 0, but differently under O = 3 (update line 7 in the Makefile). Under O = 3, it does not recognize 'prog {' etc. (see program.txt in the source tree).

Assuming the simplified source tree is in a directory ./stan-qi-problem and that is the current working directory of a Terminal, I do:

clear && rm parser && make parser && ./parser program.txt

I believe you mentioned that an email has gone out to the BSQ team but no response has been received. If you think it is useful to proceed with this investigation I could try to post this reproducible source tree to the BSQ team to see if that helps in getting a response (I know the tree is still more then a single main program, but testing goes pretty fast now).

A further request is whether a few list members can check this on their systems. On my MacbookPro I use below clang++ version:

Robs-15inch-2:stan-qi-problem rob$ clang++ --version
Apple LLVM version 5.0 (clang-500.1.63) (based on LLVM 3.3svn)
Target: x86_64-apple-darwin12.5.0
Thread model: posix

It would be nice to know if this is clang, clang version and/or Mac specific.

Regards,
Rob J. Goedman
goe...@icloud.com

Il 17/07/2013 00:42, Peter Li ha scritto:
> Overall, it's really up to you. Just let me know, and I'll work on
> whatever you're not doing.

It's very kind of you, but I think that a few guidelines would be useful.
I've seen that you have modified my code. If I write the code as you
like (not an issue, really) you save time. It's a matter of productivity ;-)

Yes, I can go on and write the R code. My first guidelines (Bob's
advice) are:
1) model and (stan_rdumped) data in separate files;
2) R code should run out of the box (source the script and look at
numerical and graphical results);
3) no commented out alternative code;
4) data transformation in Stan (transformed data block).

Other choices:
5) library() or stopifnot(require())?
6) saving and loading a compiled model;
7) source() or read_rdump()?
8) graphics.

My personal opinions:

5) stopifnot() could be used when a package is not part of a standard R
istallation (such as rstan, but also ggplot2!), but it could be
confusing; I'ld now leave sopifnot() to the R gurus and use library()
(Bob's advice);

6) I've used "if (!file.exists("sm.RData")) then compile&save else load"
because it's convenient, but I got a few segfaults when loading and
reloading several times the same DSO (see:
https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/0Ev3agQB4g0/pCYN2bwyabQJ).
So I'm going tu use "if (!exists(sm)) then { if
(file.exists("sm.RData")) then load else compile&save }".

7) read_rdump() is very nice, because one can write:

fit <- sampling(sm, data=read_rdump("foo.data.R"))

instead of

source("foo.data.R")
dataList <- list(...)
fit <- sampling(sm, data=dataList)

but looking at the variables could be a bit cumbersome because
read_rdump() does not read the data into the user's workspace.

8) The question is: who is the target user?
No problem if the answer is "whoever".
But if the answer was "whoever is reading ARM" then the R code should
just show how to use stan() instead of lm()/lmer()/bugs(), extract()
instead of sim(). BTW, sim() is part of the arm package, which loads
lattice :-)
Having to "think in ggplot2" instead of "think in base graphics" could
overload the target user.

However these are just my humble opinions.
If you favor, say, "sopifnot, shorter if, read_rdump, ggplot2", I'll
adapt to save your time.

Sergio

messages.subject: Re: Wald/Inverse Gaussian Distribution
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Joe. Hopefully, this indicates that adding a distribution to Stan is relatively easy if you can start with a similar distribution that is already in Stan.

There are a few more steps that need to be taken in order to incorporate this into Stan, such as writing unit tests, exposing the function to the Stan language, coding an algorithm to draw random numbers, etc. If you are interested in learning how to do this and have some familiarity with git, we can walk you through the process. If not, someone else will probably pick up your attachment and take it the rest of the way eventually.

One thing that I had mentioned on the developer list a month or so ago is that we would like to push in the direction of implementing more general distributions that have 3, 4, 5, ... parameters and include the more commonly-used distributions as special cases. Doing so provides a lot more flexibility (to the user) without much additional cost (to the developer). So, would you be willing to implement the generalized inverse Gaussian?

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generalized_inverse_Gaussian_distribution

And if you want the plain inverse Gaussian as well, just make what you have now into a one-line C++ function that calls the generalized_inverse_gaussian_log() with the appropriate restrictions on the parameters.

Thanks,
Ben

messages.body_plain:
Yes, we have the modified Bessel function.  It's not in
the current release of Stan, but is on the develop branch
in Git and will be in Stan 2.0.

You can check out our wiki for some more tips for developers.

   https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki

In particular, there's a discussion of the Git development process (which
is pretty daunting if you haven't used git at this point, but we
have step-by-step instructions), and a discussion of some tools that
might be helpful, and a discussion of what we need in addition to the
function itself in the way of doc, tests, and symbol table manipulation.

There are two ways to implement a new distribution.  The efficient,
vectorized way is illustrated with most of our distributions.  You can
also just template out the arguments and write the function itself without
calculating derivatives by hand.  It'll be quite a bit (maybe a factor of 2 to 10),
slower, but it might be a good place to start to get something working right
away -- it's always easy to go from working to optimized than the other way
around.

- Bob

messages.subject: Help speeding up Stan code?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Wonderful Stan Mailing List,

As part of a larger project, I've been working on a causal inference problem known as "model-based Instrumental Variables". I had pulled together a decent MCMC algorithm by hand, but Andy convinced me that I should try it out with Stan. I'm happy to report that I've already seen a dramatic speed-up, even though the model isn't a natural candidate for Stan---so I'm very pleased!

I'm writing because I need to greatly expand the current model (e.g., increase the number of mixture components; add in hierarchical effects; etc.). But, before I do, I want to make sure that I have the stripped-down model running as efficiently as possible. While I've done my best, I'm pretty new to Stan and generally lousy at coding. This is especially true since the model is a combination of mixture modeling and hierarchical regression. And, of course, there's the distinct possibility that I'm also making an inferential mistake...

I'm particularly interested in ways of speeding up the current "transformed parameters" section, which seems to be the slowest part. In a usual MCMC, this part is executed via data augmentation, which is obviously impossible in Stan.

Attached are (1) R script that generates fake data (based largely on an article by Imbens & Rubin, 1997) and runs the model; and (2) the stripped-down Stan model.

I really do appreciate the help from this exceptional group.

Many thanks,
Avi

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm currently trying to fit a quite complex nonlinear model using Stan. Since the parameters are interdependent the fits can fail regularly (most often with
No acceptably small step size could be found. Perhaps the posterior is not continuous?
error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done
).

I'm trying to test reparameterizations and new model configurations. I need to post-process the stan output to examine the fits, and my post-processing functions expect named parameter vectors output by Stan's extract() function.

For development and otherwise, it would be great to be able to fix (i.e. not model) a parameter value, but still have Stan output a vector of "samples" of that value. Is there a simple way to do this in a stan model file?

As a simple example, suppose I'm fitting a model with parameters a, b, and c. In my case I specify priors over the log values of those parameters then exponentiate them for the model fit.

e.g.:
log_c ~ normal(log(10), 1);
c <- exp(log_c);

** do stuff with c, a and b**

for testing, I'd like to be able to just write:
log_c <- log(10);

but have Stan still output the "parameter" log_c as a vector all of value log(10). Currently I need to alter my post-processing scripts so they don't expect the log_c parameter.

Is there a better way to do this?

Thanks for your help.

messages.body_plain:
On 7/18/13 6:19 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Thursday, July 18, 2013 8:30:09 AM UTC-4, Avi Feller wrote:
>
>     I'm particularly interested in ways of speeding up the current "transformed parameters" section, which seems to be
>     the slowest part. In a usual MCMC, this part is executed via data augmentation, which is obviously impossible in Stan.

You can tell this will be the slow part because it's N * K
exp() evals, plus N size-K sums.

...

Your code looks pretty clean (if oddly R-like in spacing
to my eyes; pardon my reversion to C++ style).

Using a sum() of an explicitly calculated vector should work.

You can make this faster:

   for(k in 1:(K-2))
     for(d in 1:D)
       gamma[k,d] ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

by vectorizing.    Same for the beta distributed normal.

   for (k in 1:(K-2))
     gamma[k] ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);

And this is most efficient as an array of vectors (whhat
you have for beta, but not gamma).  We'll eventually vectorize
this all more efficiently so you can just write gamma ~ cauchy(0,2.5)
and then the most efficient version will be a matrix.  (Sorry
it's a moving target for efficiency issues.)

> it should be a little faster if you use the softmax() function. What you have here relies on the
> auto-differentiation mechanism to do the derivatives, while most named functions in Stan have analytic derivatives. The
> auto-differentiation requires memory allocations and so forth.

I'm afraid softmax() isn't one of them, so you're unlikely
to see any speedup at all.

But it is built in, so it should be a little less error prone
than coding your own softmax in the model.

We should add faster auto-diff for softmax --- I was too lazy to
compute and code the derivatives when I coded it initially.

And you're actually taking the log of a softmax, which would
be another op that itself could be sped up and made more arithmetically
stable.  Do you really need the normalization supplied by softmax?
We only need probabilities up to a proportion, and it looks like you
get the same denominator in each term in the if either way.

For simplicity, you could pull this term

    if (cat[n] == 1)
      log_p_vec[n] <- log(theta[n,1])
                      + normal_log(y[n], beta[1] * x[n], sigma[1]);

messages.subject: Optimisation issues with two time series involving transfer function
messages.subject_clean: Optimisation issues with two time series involving transfer function
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I'm working on my honours project at the University of Auckland with Dr. Brendon Brewer. It involves modelling reverberation mapping data for Active Galactic Nuclei. More simply, the data are two time series. We need to first fit an AR(1) model to the first time series (Y1) that only has partial observations (with known measurement error), and then use this to model the second time series (Y2) which follows the first through a transfer function, whose parameter of interest is tau, the lag between the first and second time series.

The formula for the first time series is:
Y1[t] = mu + alpha * (Y1[t-1] - mu), a typical AR(1) model, with the observations y1(t) ~ Normal(Y1[t], beta^2). For the data we are using approximately 1000 points in the full Y1 time series, and we have roughly 10% of them observed (the reason for needing so many points is that we are approximating a continuous autoregressive CAR(1) model). If we apply this model to the first time series alone, STAN converges nicely and estimates the parameters very well.

The second series is where we start running into issues. We are assuming a uniform transfer function between two values, a and b, so that the value of the second series at time t, Y2[t], is the mean of the first time series between times t-a and t-b, with some other constants for variability and shift (eta and C).
The equation is:
Y2[t] = eta * ( (1 / N) * SUM(Y[t - a] : Y[t - b]) + C ), where N is the number of values in the summed interval.

The problem we are having is summing over the correct range of Y1. STAN doesn't allow subsets (as far as I can tell), so I have used an if() ... control flow to go through every Y1 value and check if the time value, t, is in the required interval.

This method is working, however the model runs quite slowly, and takes a couple of hours to analyse the data from one object, and in the end we will need to apply the model to many objects (~100).

I have attached a working STAN model, and would like to know if you have any ideas or techniques that will help achieve convergence faster. The autocorrelation is very high, however because the chains take so long to run I am hesitant to simply use a large trimming interval, so any ways to try and minimise this would very much be appreciated.

I have also included an R script (example.R) that includes the type of data we will be using, incase you want to test any ideas you have.

Thanks in advance for any help you can offer,

Tom Elliott.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Thanks so much for the thoughtful responses. I've cleaned up my code and have found a decent speed increase---so much appreciated.

On the various recommendations:
Vectorizing priors. Absolutely. This was a silly oversight on my part and was easy to fix.
Combining categories. This was an incredibly helpful suggestion and dramatically streamlined my code. Much appreciated.
Softmax. Curious that there's no speed increase from using this (I'll be on the lookout for when this makes it in a subsequent version). As a practical matter, I want the flexibility to add several terms together in each element in the vector, and this proved clunky via the current parameterization of the softmax function. Of course, it's possible that I'm just implementing it wrong...
Not normalizing probability vectors. I absolutely agree that, in theory, we only need to know probabilities up to a normalizing constant. But when I dropped the normalizing step, I kept getting non-sensical results. Normalizing the vector seems to only lead to a slight speed decrease (and the estimates themselves are substantively useful), so it's not a huge concern---though I'm wondering what exactly is going wrong.
Finally, I'm interested in what Ben has in mind on data augmentation. I know I've talked this through a bit with some of the Stan folks and we never really arrived at a sensible solution.

Thanks again for the help---and for the reassurance that my code isn't totally embarrassing (if a bit R-like; guilty as charged on that one).

Best,
Avi

Yes, "size" means vector size.  So what's happening is that
differently shaped or sized multidimensional objects are
being passed into the normal distribution at some point,
one of which appears to be three times as long as
the other.  Sure enough, here's the culprit:

   data {
     vector[D * Nstack] x[N]; // obsns

   parameters {
     vector[D] newgen_means[N];
     vector<lower=0>[D] newgen_stdvs[N];

   model {
     ...
     x[1] ~ normal(newgen_means[1], newgen_stdvs[1]);

So what you need to do is declare:

    data {
      vector[D] x[N,Nstack];
    ...
    model {
      for (ns in 1:Nstack}
        x[n,1] ~ normal(new_gen_means[1], newgen_stdvs[1]);

And the same thing for the x[n] case later.

This is just the use case we were imagining vectorizing so that you
could write what you wrote originally with the data type for
x:

   data {
      vector[D] x[N,Nstack];
   ...
  model {
     ...
     x[1] ~ normal(newgen_means[1], newgen_stdvs[1]);

I'm following up with a message about fixing our error messages.

in the wild rather than when we're doing development and know what
to look for.

messages.subject: clarifying error messages (again!)
messages.body_plain:
Dan Stowell's recent post highlighted just how opaque our
error messages can be in context:

   Informational Message: The parameter state is about to be Metropolis
   rejected due to the following underlying, non-fatal (really) issue
   (and please ignore that what comes next might say 'error'): Error in
   function stan::prob::normal_log(m): Location parameter (max size) is
   256, but must be consistent, 1 or max=768
   If the problem persists across multiple draws, you might have a
   problem with an initial state or a gradient somewhere.
   If the problem does not persist, the resulting samples will still be
   drawn from the posterior.

   Initialization failed after 100 attempts.  Try specifying initial
   values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the
   model.

I had to grep for the message in our code and then reason backwards.

What's happening is that the model is throwing an exception at every log
probability evaluation when given inconsistly shaped and sized inputs.
Therefore the initializer can't find a valid place to start.

We should find some language to clean up both of these messages
in our next release and put them in the doc.  For the first message,
we might want to add to the other suggestions:

   check that all functions and distributions have consistently sized,
   in-support arguments

and for the second message

   a function was called with arguments of different scalar, array, vector,
   or matrix types, and they were not consistently sized;  all arguments
   must be scalars or multidimensional values of the same shape;  found dimensions=
   <list of argument shapes passed in>

I'll add it to the to-do list for 2.0 on the Wiki.

- Bob

On Friday, July 19, 2013 8:08:27 PM UTC-4, Carlos wrote:
> I am trying to estimate with STAN a structural Vector Autoregressive model. In order to do it, I think that I have to modify the lp__ in the model block, but I am not sure if I am doing it properly. It seems to work, but I would like some confirmation that I am on the right track if that's possible.

This isn't optimal:

lp__ <- lp__ + 0.5*log(square(determinant(A))) + multi_normal_cholesky_log(A*col(Y,n), C + B*col(X,n), H);

First,  0.5*log(square(determinant(A))) == log_determinant(A) and the log_determinant() function is something optimized that Marcus wrote. But in your case, A is diagonal so the log determinant is just sum(log(A1)) which is much faster than doing anything on an arbitrary positive definite matrix.

Second, if H is diagonal, then you don't want to call any variant of multi_normal(). Instead subtract

(A*col(Y,n) - (C + B*col(X,n))) ./ H1 )

Then, you have to account for the log determinant of H * H' , which is just 2 * sum(log(H1)) but is multiplied by -1/2 in the multinormal log-likelihood.

So, I think it should be

lp__ <- lp__ + sum(log(A1)) - dot_self( (A*col(Y,n) - (C + B*col(X,n))) ./ H1 ) - sum(log(H1));

Ben

messages.subject: Re: Randomness during adapting causing slow sampling for chains in parallel?
messages.subject_clean: Randomness during adapting causing slow sampling for chains in parallel?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for all of the assistance everyone. Here's what has seemed to work well for me in regards to getting all chains to finish at about the same time (while maintaining good effective sample sizes):

- For all runs, use delta=0.25 and max_treedepth=5.
- Perform an initial small sample run from random inits using default amount of warmup (when I used no warmup, all samples were rejected).
- Use the estimates from the initial run as initial values to the full run.

My experience has been that the max_treedepth=5 helps keep NUTS from going for too long during adaption, and once sampling is started I still get good effective sample sizes. Your mileage may vary, although it has seemed to really help since I have high dimensions.

Not exactly sure how much the lower delta of 0.25 helped, but it seemed to be closer to a good value versus 0.5. That said, I found myself wanting to be able to set the initial step sizes for all variables (say with a list like initial values?) when using varying step sizes for each parameter. Perhaps this is on the TODO list?

Thanks again,
Ryan

On 7/20/13 4:43 PM, Ryan wrote:
> Thanks for all of the assistance everyone. Here's what has seemed to work well for me in regards to getting all chains
> to finish at about the same time (while maintaining good effective sample sizes):
>
> - For all runs, use delta=0.25 and max_treedepth=5.

That's probably enough tree depth for most problems.  It only
allows 32 leapfrog steps and some problems require more.

> - Perform an initial small sample run from random inits using default amount of warmup (when I used no warmup, all
> samples were rejected).
> - Use the estimates from the initial run as initial values to the full run.

The problem with this approach is that it doesn't use diffuse inits, which
we feel are important for convergence monitoring.  The danger is
that if you start all the samples from the same point, you won't find
different modes or non-identifiability, or perhaps detect if you're
exploring enough of the parameter space.  Also, if the init doesn't get
to a good place, all the chains will suffer.

We've been thinking a good strategy might be to do something like let
warmup get close to a solution, then randomize a bit.  The problem is
that of scale.

> My experience has been that the max_treedepth=5 helps keep NUTS from going for too long during adaption, and once
> sampling is started I still get good effective sample sizes. Your mileage may vary, although it has seemed to really
> help since I have high dimensions.
>
> Not exactly sure how much the lower delta of 0.25 helped, but it seemed to be closer to a good value versus 0.5. That
> said, I found myself wanting to be able to set the initial step sizes for all variables (say with a list like initial
> values?) when using varying step sizes for each parameter. Perhaps this is on the TODO list?

Yes, it's on the to-do list.  I'm not sure if it's in the 2.0
refactor or not.  Michael's rewritten most of the command structure
to make this kind of thing easier to generalize across samplers
and optimizers.

- Bob

>     we feel are important for convergence monitoring.  The danger is
>     that if you start all the samples from the same point, you won't find
>     different modes or non-identifiability, or perhaps detect if you're
>     exploring enough of the parameter space.  Also, if the init doesn't get
>     to a good place, all the chains will suffer.
>
>     We've been thinking a good strategy might be to do something like let
>     warmup get close to a solution, then randomize a bit.  The problem is
>     that of scale.
>
>
> I wonder if instead of using the initial mean for all chains I were to use a random sample from the initial run? This
> wouldn't be as overdisperesed like random inits, but it also wouldn't be the same for all chains. Perhaps this could
> help get closer to the right place for all chains. Any ideas if this kind of strategy would be almost as good as random
> inits?

We've been discussing various adaptation strategies like this
in our meetings and still haven't figured out the right thing
to do.

A random sample from a single chain still defeats the purpose of
overdispersed starting points, which is to provide a sanity check on the
model and its computation.

For well-behaved models, it shouldn't matter where you start.

We want to concentrate on getting from any initial point to
the typical set of the distribution so we can start sampling
and properly adapting.

But clearly we're not there yet, which is why some chains
are so much slower than others.  In fact, we've found the slow
chain when running four chains often dominates the compute time.
And it makes compute time highly variable on a per-chain basis.

One of the problems with the strategy of concentrating on a single
chain from the start is that you might pick the bad starting point.

Another approach we've been discussing is running each chain
for a fixed time rather than a fixed number of iterations.  Then
we get an implicit downweighting of the slow-to-converge chains if
we weight by number of iterations.  We're still working out the details.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Randomness during adapting causing slow sampling for chains in parallel?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Randomness during adapting causing slow sampling for chains in parallel?
messages.body_plain:
I am extremely dubious of this approach -- I'm pretty sure you're just producing biased samples.  Here's what I think is going on:

The main problem I'm seeing in adaptation is when the covariance is strongly position-dependent.  If NUTS can't cross the entirety of the typical set in one trajectory (as is common in hierarchical models without the Matt trick) then the empirical covariance used in the adaptation won't be the global covariance and the post-update chain will slow to a crawl once it's left the region of the previous adaptation update.

What you've done here is to essentially make the problem even worse.  By decreasing the maximum tree depth and lowering the target acceptance rate you're inducing random walk behavior that drastically slows the exploration of the sampler.  This keeps the chain in a small neighborhood where the covariance is approximately constant and the adaptation appears to be working fine.

On Jul 20, 2013, at 9:43 PM, Ryan <sick...@gmail.com> wrote:

messages.body_plain:
Yeah, you could set the tree depth to zero but then you're not taking advantage of HMC.  The problem here is not NUTS but rather the adaptation -- in Stan 2.0 you can run the samplers with a global step size adaptation, but until then you can try setting the step size by hand to avoid the adaptation.  Incidently, I believe 2^10 was set as the default to prevent NUTS from running for huge lengths of time without being the user being made aware of potential problems.

The biggest problem is that poor adaptation can actually bias the sampler by preventing the chain from visiting regions of high curvature (or extremely different curvature from the current point), and that won't show up in ESS/Rhat calculations.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How does STAN define priors on covariance matrices?
messages.body_plain:
Any variable declared in Stan without a prior is given
a uniform prior on its support.  For covariance matrices,
that's an improper prior.

The unconstrained parameterization is a Cholesky factor with
log-transformed diagonal.  The Jacobian adjustment
to make it uniform on covariance (symmetric, positive-definite
in Stan) matrices is described in the manual near the end in the
variable transform chapter.

We'd love to hear about any publications with models fit
using Stan.

- Bob

On 7/22/13 9:34 AM, Peter Li wrote:
> Actually, can't I just pull random generations from the samples themselves, since the simulations themselves are
> posterior simulations?

Those are draws from the posterior, not simulated data.

Suppose you have data y and parameters mu and sigma for a simple
normal.

   data {
     ...
     vector[N] y;
   model {
     ...
     y ~ normal(mu,sigma);
   }

then you want to generate new data y-twiddle, by

   y_twiddle ~ normal(mu,sigma);

You can do this in the generated quantities block:

generated quantities {
   vector[N_twiddle] y_twiddle;

   for (i in 1:size(y_twiddle))
     y_twiddle[i] <- normal_rng(mu,sigma);

where mu and sigma are the parameters fit by the model.

- Bob

> It was a stupid error of mine...
> My model:

> data {
>    vector[N] x;
>    ...
> }
> transformed data {
>    real x_mean;
>    vector[N] centered_x;
>    centered_x <- x - centered_x; // !!!
>    ...
> }
> etc.
>
> The model compiled, sampling took a loooong time, results were meaningless.
> Are such errors intended to be caught?

I'm afraid there's nothing in place to catch the use
of uninitialized variables in vector operations.  It
would slow them down considerably.

Some of the more complex functions trap and report on errors.
All of the distributions do.  None of the C++ library functions
or built-in operators do.

We should develop a diagnostic in the parser that finds
the use of variables before they are defined.
I'll put that on the to-do list.  It wouldn't be able to catch
everything, but the example you have could be caught.

- Bob

started so I just have a few things going.

Anyhow, I know there are better ways to parameterize the model.
However, I have this set-up to mimic the standard frequentist
mixed-model to help the transition for my students. If anyone is
interested, I'd welcome alterations to the code that would make it
better or additional examples. Also if I have anything wrong, I'd
appreciate corrections.

Hope this is useful.

Best,
Scott

messages.subject: normal() + comma = normal_log()
messages.body_plain:
Another stupid error of mine:

model {
  z_log_earn ~ normal(z_beta[1] + z_beta[2] * z_height, + z_beta[3] * z_male, z_sigma);
}

I left a comma after z_height, when I added the last predictor.
The model did non compile, of course, but I got this message:

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
no matches for function name="normal_log"

It looks a bit strange, doesn't it?

Thanks

Sergio

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] normal() + comma = normal_log()
messages.body_plain:
On 7/27/13 11:45 AM, sp_r...@yahoo.it wrote:
> Another stupid error of mine:
>
> model {
>    z_log_earn ~ normal(z_beta[1] + z_beta[2] * z_height, + z_beta[3] * z_male, z_sigma);
> }
>
> I left a comma after z_height, when I added the last predictor.
> The model did non compile, of course, but I got this message:
>
> DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
> no matches for function name="normal_log"
>
> It looks a bit strange, doesn't it?

The problem is that (+ a * b) is a well-formed
expression, so the parser took you to be specifying
three arguments to normal().

In general,

    y ~ foo(theta1,...,thetaN);

compiles as:

    lp__ <- lp__ + foo_log(y,theta1,...,thetaN)

So the function getting called is the _log version.
We should try to make that message clearer.  Someone else
already filed an issue about changing our manual to make this
relationship clearer in the doc of every distribution.

- Bob

I'm very sorry to hear that.  Windows has given us no end
of problems on the development side, too, because the entire
open source C++ toolchain is so much weaker.

You definitely need to get Rcpp working before you can
install RStan.   When it's sorted out, could you please post
back here with what the problem was and what needed to be done
to fix it?  We're trying to build up the expertise to help more
people through Windows installs in the future.

For getting help from the Rcpp list, I'd suggest trying
to include more information on exactly what you did in terms
of installing and uninstalling applications.  I don't know
enough about Windows to tell you how to do this exactly,
but your PATH will also be important.  And as Ben said, this
looks like it may be a permissions issue, so there's the
matter of how you are logged in (as a regular user or admin),
which version of Windows you're using, which version of RTools,
what kind of shell you're using, and so on.

> Hope that someone who has
> experience this can give some hints on how to solve it.

I'm afraid that's not me.  The only hint I saw online is that
it may have something to do with the R_HOME environment variable,
from Dirk's blog:  http://dirk.eddelbuettel.com/blog/2012/11/05/

I hope the Rcpp list or someone else here can help, but
as Ben says, you're currently hung up on installing Rcpp, which
is a pre-requisite for RStan.

- Bob

what operating system(s) do members of the stan development team use??

On Wed, Jul 31, 2013 at 11:19 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

>
>
> On 7/31/13 8:48 AM, Eric Chan wrote:
> > Hi Ben,
> >
> > Thank you very much for the help. I have tried to reinstall everything without the space and start R with the admin
> > privileges. However, I experience the same problem. I have tried to post question to the Rcpp list and hope to get a
> > reply soon. I have spent whole day working on it and want to use RStan as soon as possible.
>
> I'm very sorry to hear that.  Windows has given us no end
> of problems on the development side, too, because the entire
> open source C++ toolchain is so much weaker.
>
> You definitely need to get Rcpp working before you can
> install RStan.   When it's sorted out, could you please post
> back here with what the problem was and what needed to be done
> to fix it?  We're trying to build up the expertise to help more
> people through Windows installs in the future.
>
> For getting help from the Rcpp list, I'd suggest trying
> to include more information on exactly what you did in terms
> of installing and uninstalling applications.  I don't know
> enough about Windows to tell you how to do this exactly,
> but your PATH will also be important.  And as Ben said, this
> looks like it may be a permissions issue, so there's the
> matter of how you are logged in (as a regular user or admin),
> which version of Windows you're using, which version of RTools,
> what kind of shell you're using, and so on.
>
>
> > Hope that someone who has
> > experience this can give some hints on how to solve it.
>
> I'm afraid that's not me.  The only hint I saw online is that
> it may have something to do with the R_HOME environment variable,
> from Dirk's blog:  http://dirk.eddelbuettel.com/blog/2012/11/05/
>
> I hope the Rcpp list or someone else here can help, but
> as Ben says, you're currently hung up on installing Rcpp, which
> is a pre-requisite for RStan.
>
> - Bob

>

Thank you, Terrance Savitsky

On Wed, Jul 31, 2013 at 3:47 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

>
> And I think we all use emacs or vim and a shell for most
> everything other than R.
>
> Our integration server runs Jenkins on Windows, so we do test
> Windows operation.
>

My main development is done on a Mac. If we have Windows issues or when my machine is in for repair, I develop on a Windows machine: Windows 7 Enterprise, Rtools 2.15. I use emacs on both Windows and Mac for development. There is a Stan emacs mode that has syntax highlighting and smart indentation for Stan models: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan-mode

Daniel
